analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deductions for executive pay above $1 million at public companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from April 2015 until the 114th Congress ended, so corporations kept deducting unlimited performance-based executive pay.
analysis.plain_summary: Current tax law already bars publicly held companies from deducting each executive's salary above $1 million, but the rule is full of holes: it exempts "performance-based" pay and commissions, covers only the top five officers, doesn't apply to former executives, and misses some SEC-regulated companies. This bill would close all of those loopholes, so companies could no longer write off unlimited multimillion-dollar bonuses and stock payouts. That would raise corporate taxes and remove a tax subsidy for outsized executive compensation.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently make up the difference when public corporations deduct enormous executive payouts from their taxable income; the federal Treasury would collect more corporate tax revenue, and shareholders would gain modestly from governance pressure on pay. Employees at public companies might also benefit over time if firms respond by restraining top pay.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the $1 million cap on deductible executive pay to any current or former officer, director, or employee of a public company, closing the loophole that stopped the clock once someone retired.

Eliminates the exemption for commission-based pay and for pay tied to a performance goal, the two channels corporations used to deduct unlimited multimillion-dollar bonuses and stock awards on top of the $1 million salary cap.
Applies the cap to every corporation registered with the SEC or required to file reports to investors, rather than only the narrow set of companies covered under current law.
Directs the Treasury Department to write the rules needed to enforce the expanded cap, including reporting requirements, so companies cannot simply relabel pay to evade it.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations and their highest-paid executives. Companies would lose deductions for executive compensation above $1 million per person once bonuses, commissions, and performance awards counted toward the cap, increasing their federal tax bills. Executives would face pressure toward leaner pay packages.
analysis.who_pays_short: Publicly traded corporations and top executives

drawbacks.text: The performance-based exemption was originally justified as encouraging companies to tie executive pay to results; eliminating it removes that tax incentive to link pay to measurable goals, which supporters of the exemption argue could blunt performance incentives.

The cost falls on corporations, and some of it could ultimately be passed along to shareholders through lower after-tax returns or to workers if companies redirect compensation budgets, though the bill's main effect is to unwind a deduction, not to raise wages or prices directly.

Adding former officers, directors, and employees to the covered group and requiring Treasury to write new reporting rules adds compliance complexity for companies that must track pay across decades of retirees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a fairly straightforward loophole closer: it takes an existing, widely known rule — the $1 million cap on deductible executive pay — and removes the carve-outs that made it largely toothless for the biggest payouts. The cost is real but concentrated: higher tax bills for large public companies and less rich pay packages for executives. The benefit to ordinary people is indirect but genuine, since taxpayers effectively foot part of every deductible executive bonus. The design is sound; the main honest caveat is that the effect on actual executive pay levels depends on how companies respond, and the added compliance burden on retirees' deferred pay is a fair complaint.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the bill on April 29, 2015, with Senator Richard Blumenthal signing on as an original sponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over the tax code.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor during the two-year Congress.

Because the bill died without enactment, the exemptions for performance-based, commission-based, and former-executive pay remained in the tax code, and public companies continued deducting compensation above $1 million per executive.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded corporations and their highest-paid executives are better off, because the tax deductions for multimillion-dollar performance bonuses and commissions survived untouched. The Treasury continues to forgo that revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big public companies and their executives

for.name: Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's other original sponsor at introduction

for.name: 9 senators
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors — 8 Democrats and 1 Independent

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Orrin Hatch (R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred on April 29, 2015; it sat for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Republican Senate majority
against.what_they_did: Allowed no floor action on a bill that would raise taxes on large public corporations; no member of the Republican conference cosponsored it

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so there is no roll call to measure; the bill's ten sponsors and cosponsors were all Democrats or independents, with no Republican support in the record.

industries.note: These companies currently deduct executive pay above $1 million whenever it is labeled performance-based or commission-based, a write-off paid for by other taxpayers. The bill would end those deductions, raising their federal tax bills. Their interest in keeping the loophole runs against the public's interest in a broader tax base.

industries.industry: Top corporate executives at public companies
industries.note: Executives would face stronger company-side pressure toward leaner pay once the unlimited performance-pay deduction disappeared, since every dollar above $1 million would become a nondeductible cost. Former executives would also be covered for the first time.

industries.industry: Executive compensation consultants and deferred-compensation plan administrators
industries.note: The bill would create new work structuring compliant pay packages and reporting to Treasury, but would also shrink the market for designing tax-favored performance awards for former employees. The net effect on this service industry is genuinely two-sided.
